newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus bank chief held, finance minister resigns.
newsitem.headline: Belarus bank chief held, finance minister resigns.

text.p: The head of Belarus's central bank has been sacked and arrested in connection with a corruption charge and President Alexander Lukashenko has also accepted his finance minister's resignation, state media said on Tuesday.
A statement read on the former Soviet republic's national radio said central bank head Tamara Vinnikova had been detained by police after being accused of "damages to the state of major proportions".
State television later quoted the president's press service as saying Lukashenko had appointed a new Finance Minister, Nikolai Rumas, in place of Pavel Dik, who had asked to leave.
Dik's resignation followed a string of changes in Lukashenko's cabinet in recent months. There was no indication it was connected to Vinnikova's sacking.
Lukashenko has sacked or accepted the resignations of several ministers and top officials recently, particularly since winning a constitutional referendum in November.

Following the vote, which he won by a landslide but critics said was fraudulent, Lukashenko rewrote the constitution to create an upper house of parliament and renamed the "cabinet of ministers" as "council of ministers".
Lukashenko told the first session on Monday of the new upper house of parliament that Vinnikova, 46, was one of three candidates to head the central bank, indicating he was thinking of removing her.
He mentioned nothing of impending criminal proceedings but said commercial banks had spoken against her.
"I cannot help but take account of the opinion of the leaders of banks of such stature," he told the chamber.
Acting Prime Minister Sergei Ling had predicted her dismissal saying that although a specialist "she perhaps lacks experience, broad vision and administrative capabilities".
Vinnikova replaced Stanislav Bogdankevich, a reformer effectively forced from office by Lukashenko to the dismay of Western financial institutions seeking change.
She had earlier been head of the large Belarus Bank, which merged with the state savings bank in August 1995 to create the largest bank in the country of 10 million.
Vinnikova had initially been an unquestioning supporter of Lukashenko's reluctant approach to market reforms when appointed, but over time objected to many of his policies.
She opposed Lukashenko's decision to lower refinancing rates without consulting the central bank and the creation of a corridor to regulate the rate of the Belarussian rouble.

New Finance Minister Rumas was Dik's deputy and has considerable experience within the ministry, running talks with the International Monetary Fund which has suspended credits to Belarus pending faster reforms.

Dik, who served as finance minister since Lukashenko became president in 1994, told Reuters this week that monthly inflation in January would leap to more than 10 percent from a planned two percent and warned of "strong inflationary expectations".
